questions.stem: The left model shows a normal three-cusp valve; the right model shows a two-cusp variant. What is the clinical significance of the configuration on the right?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A congenital bicuspid aortic valve, which predisposes to early calcification and premature aortic stenosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: A normal variant with no increased risk of valve disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: An acquired rheumatic deformity with commissural fusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: A prosthetic mechanical valve orientation

choices.label: E
choices.text: A quadricuspid valve that causes chronic regurgitation only

explanation.summary: A bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital cardiac anomaly; abnormal leaflet mechanics accelerate degenerative calcification, so stenosis typically presents decades earlier than in trileaflet valves.
explanation.whyCorrect: A bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital cardiac anomaly; abnormal leaflet mechanics accelerate degenerative calcification, so stenosis typically presents decades earlier than in trileaflet valves.

questions.stem: These CT angiographic reconstructions of the coronary vasculature show dense, bright deposits (arrowheads) near the aortic root. What do these represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Metastatic tumor deposits in the myocardium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fresh intraluminal thrombus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Air embolism within the coronary tree

choices.label: D
choices.text: Coronary artery / aortic valve calcification

choices.label: E
choices.text: Contrast extravasation from a ruptured vessel

explanation.summary: The very high-attenuation (bright white) foci on CT are calcium deposits. Coronary and aortic valve calcification commonly accompany degenerative aortic stenosis and are quantified as a calcium score.
explanation.whyCorrect: The very high-attenuation (bright white) foci on CT are calcium deposits. Coronary and aortic valve calcification commonly accompany degenerative aortic stenosis and are quantified as a calcium score.

questions.stem: This transverse gross section of the heart from a patient with long-standing aortic stenosis shows a characteristic ventricular remodeling pattern. What is it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amyloid infiltration causing a stiff non-hypertrophied wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eccentric hypertrophy with a dilated thin-walled chamber

choices.label: C
choices.text: Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with a thickened wall and preserved/reduced chamber size

choices.label: D
choices.text: Right ventricular hypertrophy from pulmonary hypertension

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acute transmural myocardial infarction with wall thinning

explanation.summary: Chronic pressure overload from a stenotic aortic valve drives parallel sarcomere addition, producing concentric LV hypertrophy: a markedly thickened wall without chamber dilation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic pressure overload from a stenotic aortic valve drives parallel sarcomere addition, producing concentric LV hypertrophy: a markedly thickened wall without chamber dilation.

questions.stem: This gross specimen viewed from above shows the thickened, rigid, nodular cusps of the indicated valve with a narrowed central orifice. What is the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aortic valve endocarditis with vegetations

choices.label: B
choices.text: Myxomatous mitral valve prolapse

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rheumatic mitral stenosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal pliable tricuspid aortic valve

choices.label: E
choices.text: Calcific aortic valve stenosis

explanation.summary: The cusps are heaped up with rigid calcific nodules that restrict opening, reducing the effective orifice area. This degenerative calcific process is the leading cause of aortic stenosis in older adults.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cusps are heaped up with rigid calcific nodules that restrict opening, reducing the effective orifice area. This degenerative calcific process is the leading cause of aortic stenosis in older adults.

questions.stem: This series progresses from a normal valve to severe disease. What structural process drives the narrowing of the valve orifice shown left to right?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Progressive fibrocalcific thickening of the cusps that stiffens them and reduces the opening area

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fatty streak deposition within the lumen only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fusion of cusps by fibrin-platelet vegetations from infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dilation of the aortic annulus stretching the leaflets apart

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fibrous shortening of the chordae tendineae

explanation.summary: Aortic sclerosis (leaflet thickening/calcium without obstruction) advances to stenosis as calcific nodules accumulate on the cusps, progressively immobilizing them and shrinking the systolic orifice.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aortic sclerosis (leaflet thickening/calcium without obstruction) advances to stenosis as calcific nodules accumulate on the cusps, progressively immobilizing them and shrinking the systolic orifice.

questions.stem: The shaded left ventricular pressure-volume loop shows the change produced when afterload is increased (as in aortic stenosis). What is the effect on stroke volume?

choices.label: A
choices.text: End-diastolic volume falls while stroke volume is preserved

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stroke volume is unchanged because preload compensates fully

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isovolumetric relaxation is eliminated, raising output

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stroke volume rises as the aorta accepts more blood

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stroke volume falls because the ventricle must generate higher pressure to eject, narrowing the loop

explanation.summary: A pressure-overload state raises the pressure at which the aortic valve opens, so ejection occurs against a higher load. For a given contractility the loop narrows and stroke volume decreases.
explanation.whyCorrect: A pressure-overload state raises the pressure at which the aortic valve opens, so ejection occurs against a higher load. For a given contractility the loop narrows and stroke volume decreases.

questions.stem: Comparing the two phonocardiographic tracings across the cardiac cycle, what is the characteristic murmur configuration of the upper (aortic stenosis) tracing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A continuous machinery murmur spanning systole and diastole

choices.label: B
choices.text: A late diastolic presystolic rumble before S1

choices.label: C
choices.text: An early diastolic decrescendo murmur after S2

choices.label: D
choices.text: A crescendo-decrescendo (diamond-shaped) systolic ejection murmur between S1 and S2

choices.label: E
choices.text: A uniform holosystolic (plateau) murmur that obscures S2

explanation.summary: Aortic stenosis produces a mid-systolic ejection murmur whose intensity rises then falls (diamond shape) as flow peaks then wanes; contrast with the plateau holosystolic murmur of mitral regurgitation shown below.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aortic stenosis produces a mid-systolic ejection murmur whose intensity rises then falls (diamond shape) as flow peaks then wanes; contrast with the plateau holosystolic murmur of mitral regurgitation shown below.

questions.stem: This survival curve for the natural history of aortic stenosis stays high for decades then drops sharply. What clinical event marks the inflection point after which survival collapses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The development of left atrial enlargement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Progression from a bicuspid to a tricuspid valve

choices.label: C
choices.text: The onset of symptoms (angina, syncope, or heart failure)

choices.label: D
choices.text: The appearance of valvular calcification on imaging

choices.label: E
choices.text: The first detection of a systolic murmur

explanation.summary: Aortic stenosis is asymptomatic for years; once symptoms appear, average survival is only ~2-5 years (heart failure ~2, syncope ~3, angina ~5), making symptom onset the trigger for valve replacement.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aortic stenosis is asymptomatic for years; once symptoms appear, average survival is only ~2-5 years (heart failure ~2, syncope ~3, angina ~5), making symptom onset the trigger for valve replacement.
